item.title: Houthis claim six attacks across Saudi Arabia — and Syria is now sending military advisers to Riyadh
item.description:
The Houthis claimed six attacks on Saudi airports and oil facilities on Thursday, according to a statement from their military spokesman Yahya Saree — targeting the Ras Tanura oil refinery with a ballistic missile, an Aramco facility in Abqaiq, King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh with multiple missiles, King Fahd International Airport in Dammam with a drone, the Rabigh oil refinery with a ballistic missile, and a Saudi military headquarters in the Najran region. There was no independent corroboration of the group's claims. The Saudi-led coalition said its air defences intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles fired toward Riyadh on Thursday; Saudi Civil Defence said shrapnel from the interception wounded one Saudi citizen and damaged a house and a vehicle. The Arab League condemned an attempted Houthi missile attack targeting the Madinah region on Friday, calling it a serious escalation.
The attacks came despite a rare meeting earlier this week in Tehran between senior Saudi and Iranian officials, after which both sides agreed to resolve regional differences through dialogue. Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan all sent high-level representatives to the Tehran meeting, hosted by Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei and attended by Saudi Defence Minister Khalid bin Salman. Iran's press release said participants agreed to continue discussions on peace and security; Saudi Arabia's foreign ministry stressed opening negotiation channels to prevent a return to escalation. The Houthis kept firing anyway.
Riyadh is meanwhile widening its circle of helpers. Reuters reported Friday that Syria is aiding Saudi Arabia with military advice and training, and has sent a limited number of military personnel to the kingdom, according to two Syrian military sources and a senior US official. Syrian advisers and training teams are travelling to Saudi Arabia to help train Saudi and Yemeni units, and joint training exercises are under way in both countries. The move follows a Saudi-Syrian defence cooperation deal signed Wednesday during Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa's visit to Riyadh, and Turkey's ratification on Thursday of the Mecca defence pact. A senior Syrian diplomat cautioned that "any suggestion of military deployments at this stage is premature," and Washington has urged Damascus to move cautiously, warning that any Syrian deployment to help in the Yemen war risks embroiling the country in the wider regional war. Saudi authorities also warned Friday of a possible danger in the Yanbu oil hub as Houthi attacks persist.
The Houthis say their operations target Saudi oil facilities and military bases only, and deny targeting holy sites — the coalition has repeatedly accused them of launching drones toward Mecca and Medina. Riyadh's position is that the strikes are an assault on civilian infrastructure and the kingdom's sovereignty, and it is leaning on the new Mecca pact partners and now Syria for support. Inside Yemen, the internationally recognised government has called on the UN Security Council to take "deterrent and punitive measures" to stop Houthi attacks on Aden International Airport, and fighting and the siege around Taiz continue.
For ordinary people, the pattern is now daily: air-raid warnings in Riyadh and Najran, shrapnel falling on homes, airports under threat, and a war inside Yemen that keeps getting worse — the Rasd Organization for Rights and Freedoms warns about 1,110 kidney-failure patients in besieged Taiz face dialysis shortages. The diplomacy in Tehran produced words about dialogue; the missiles kept flying the same day.
In short: the Houthis claimed six attacks across Saudi Arabia on Thursday — refineries, airports and a military HQ — with no independent confirmation, while the coalition says it intercepted missiles over Riyadh and the Arab League condemned an attempt on the Madinah region. Syria is now sending military advisers to help Riyadh, and the Tehran dialogue produced no pause in the firing.
Sources:
Source: aljazeeranews-3fuh52rgrl.edgeone.app.

item.title: OpenSSH "sshole" — CVE-2026-123158, exploited in the wild within 9 hours of disclosure
item.description:
The flaw lets remote attackers log into passwordless accounts on Alpine Linux and other musl-based systems by submitting an oversized password (257–1,024 bytes): musl's crypt() returns '*' for the overlong password, which matches accounts whose stored password field is also '*' — the standard marker for "no password login."
Threat intel firm Previdian reported Friday that its sensors saw the first attempt less than nine hours after the CVE was published, and confirmed successful root access on a honeypot running real Alpine Linux and OpenSSH — eight attempts total, all from one Japan-based IP (89.116.89[.]18). No production compromises have been reported.
The fix is OpenSSH 10.6p2, released November 5, with Alpine pushing patched packages for every branch the same day. If you run Alpine or other musl systems, update or set PasswordAuthentication no now.
Source: helpnetsecurity.com.

item.title: New CISA KEV addition today: SonicWall SonicOS SSLVPN, CVE-2026-19868 (CVSS 7.5)
item.description:
CISA added the flaw Friday based on evidence of active exploitation.
A weakness in SonicOS SSLVPN may let a user with valid credentials for an alternate authentication method bypass SAML authentication controls — including SAML-enforced MFA. Affected: SonicOS 7.3.3-7015 and older, and 8.2.2-8015 and older.
Federal remediation deadline: November 20. CISA has not named an actor or the scale of exploitation.
The catalog now stands at 1,769 entries.
Source: windowsforum.com.

Federal remediation deadline: November 20. CISA has not named an actor or the scale of exploitation.

The catalog now stands at 1,769 entries.

Source: windowsforum.com — Read the full article

item.title: US agencies warned Friday to harden cold-chain systems
item.description:
Five US agencies (CISA, FBI, HHS, USDA, DOT) told operators on November 5 to harden refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems, following the remotely triggered defrost attacks on European supermarkets and an attempt on three French plasma stores (EFS, hit November 2).
Take controllers off the internet, isolate them on their own VLAN, and alert on setpoints outside safe ranges.
Source: cyber.mag212.com.

item.title: Courts: Brand faces 6–9 years, say lawyers — sentencing Monday
item.description:
Russell Brand spent his first night in custody in HMP Wandsworth after Thursday's convictions (one rape, three sexual assaults).
Sentencing is Monday, November 9. The Bar Council chair, Kirsty Brimelow, told Sky News she expects "between six and nine years"; barrister Eleanor Laws KC, speaking on *The Trial* podcast, put it at at least 10 years.
Judge Joel Bennathan has already told Brand to expect a "significant custodial term." The Metropolitan Police investigation into two further rape allegations continues, with files before prosecutors.
No fresh developments on the FTC v. Amazon cases, the Netanyahu trial or the Murdaugh retrial (next hearing November 13).
Source: dispatchtimes.com.

item.title: Trump says he'll decide "soon" whether to resume all-out war on Iran — as Qatar pushes a two-day deal and he phones the Emir
item.description:
President Donald Trump said Thursday he will soon decide whether to order a new round of major strikes on Iran, after meeting his top national security advisers on the issue for the first time since the midterm elections. "Now we will make a decision," he told reporters in the Oval Office, adding: "I would rather not destroy the rest of the country if possible, but maybe I will have to. You'll know soon enough." The meeting was part of his weekly intelligence briefing, according to two US officials cited by Axios, and came after White House meetings on a possible resumption of military operations on Wednesday and Thursday.
Trump is weighing three options, Axios reports: launching new strikes, continuing to strangle Iran economically through sanctions and the naval blockade, or cutting a deal that includes significant concessions to the Iranians. He framed the choice around the nuclear question — whether to go further with strikes to ensure Iran's nuclear program is dead and "it will never happen again" — while stressing US forces are ready: "If we have to do the rest of the Iran thing, we're very much locked and loaded." US Central Command is finalizing preparations for a possible resumption of major combat operations, a US official said, though it has not received a new directive from Washington. A third carrier strike group, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, is heading to the region but stops in Singapore on Friday and is not expected to reach Central Command's area before mid-November.
Diplomacy is running in parallel, and it moved fast on Thursday. Qatari mediators are discussing a draft two-day confidence-building proposal with both sides: on day one, the US would lift its naval blockade and release some of Iran's frozen funds, and Iran would invite International Atomic Energy Agency inspectors to the bombed nuclear sites; on day two, the Strait of Hormuz would reopen, and nuclear talks would resume, focused on Iran's stockpile of highly enriched uranium. Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi held multiple calls Thursday with mediators from Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, the UAE, Oman and Egypt, and a senior Iranian official said Tehran sent a nuclear proposal to Washington through Qatar on Thursday. On Friday morning, Trump called Qatar's Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani — a call Trump initiated, according to Qatar's state news agency — to discuss de-escalation efforts; the Emir stressed continued dialogue, no further escalation, and protection of navigation in the strait and energy supplies. CBS News confirmed the call.
The two sides are still far apart, and each is publicly setting conditions the other has rejected. Iran's Supreme National Security Council secretary Mohsen Rezaei met Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Kremlin on Thursday, delivered a message from Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, and said afterward that Iran announced seven conditions to the Americans — including lifting sanctions, releasing frozen assets, compensation for war damage and ending the blockade — and that "until the Americans fulfill our seven conditions, neither the Strait of Hormuz will be opened nor will there be any negotiations." Putin said he is ready to try to help end the war. Washington has rejected several of the conditions and insists Iran's nuclear program be permanently dismantled. Vice President JD Vance has emerged as a leading advocate of diplomacy over renewed strikes, and has publicly blamed the war as a primary cause of the Republicans' midterm defeats; Trump has acknowledged higher gasoline prices tied to the conflict contributed to those losses. Iranian military officials have warned any new US attack would draw retaliation against US targets without geographic limits.
Meanwhile the shipping war goes on. Iran reported three more tankers damaged on Thursday, and the UK maritime agency UKMTO says incidents are running close to October's record pace of 35 vessels. One new detail: the Greek-operated, Marshall Islands-flagged tanker Velos Sapphire, struck by two unidentified projectiles about 50 nautical miles north of Qatar late Wednesday, has one seafarer missing — maritime security sources say the crew member was killed, though the International Maritime Organization has not confirmed a fatality. Iran has also reshuffled its blacklist of vessels accused of breaching its transit rules, leaving 239 ships on it, and the Joint Maritime Information Centre recorded four attacks in the strait in a 96-hour window from November 1–3, keeping its threat rating at severe. The IMO counts 129 confirmed maritime incidents in the region since the conflict began, with 24 seafarer deaths.
For ordinary people, the stakes are visible at the pump and in the markets. Brent crude traded around $99.90–$100.30 a barrel on Friday morning, up about 1.5–2% on the fresh tanker attacks, but still heading for a roughly 12% weekly decline after Wednesday's near-10% crash on hopes of a deal. Oil shipments through the strait are running below 60% of capacity, and US diesel reserves are below 100 million barrels for the first time in more than 20 years, with diesel around $6.27 a gallon — about 75% higher than a year ago. Gulf states are watching anxiously: the war is in its ninth month, and whether Trump picks strikes, pressure or a deal will shape fuel prices, shipping and the region's security for months.
In short: Trump says a decision on resuming major strikes on Iran is coming soon, with strikes, economic pressure or a Qatari-brokered deal all on the table. Qatar's two-day proposal — blockade lifted and frozen funds released, then Hormuz reopened — is being discussed, Iran has sent its own nuclear proposal, and Trump spoke to the Emir on Friday. But Iran says no talks until its seven conditions are met, and the tanker attacks and the missing seafarer on the Velos Sapphire show the shooting hasn't stopped while the diplomacy plays out.
Sources:
Source: newscentraltv.com.

item.title: Ukraine: Russia launches 227 drones overnight as both sides keep hitting each other's energy
item.description:
Russia launched 227 drones at Ukraine overnight into Friday, Ukraine's Air Force reported — Shaheds, jet-powered Shaheds, Gerbera decoys and Parodiya decoys — and air defences had shot down or neutralized 196 of them by 8 a.m. local time, including 70 jet-powered models, with the attack still ongoing at that point. Drones struck 14 locations and debris fell in eight more. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy put the figure at 210 strike drones, about 140 of them Shaheds, and said: "Russia continues to attack our energy sector, critical infrastructure, and civilian facilities."
The strikes hit the power grid hardest. An energy facility was struck in Bila Tserkva, in the Kyiv region, and Deputy Energy Minister Artem Nekrasov said new outages hit seven regions overnight and Friday morning — Vinnytsia, Dnipropetrovsk, Zhytomyr, Zaporizhzhia, Kyiv, Kharkiv and Chernihiv — with the capital region worst affected, where repair crews had to partially shut down the local grid because of heavy damage. In the Kharkiv region, railway infrastructure was attacked and traction substations hit, leaving thousands of families without electricity. A Russian drone attack damaged port infrastructure in Odesa and wounded at least two people, damaging two high-rise residential buildings; in Kherson, one person was killed and eight injured over the past day. Russia's Defence Ministry said it intercepted 142 Ukrainian drones between Thursday night and Friday morning.
Ukraine hit back at Russian energy and military targets the same night. Ukraine's General Staff said its forces struck two ammunition depots in occupied Zaporizhzhia — near Melitopol and Khliborobne — a drone command post near Chasiv Yar and a fuel depot near Luhanske in occupied Donetsk. Monitoring channels reported Ukrainian drones also struck the Afipsky oil refinery in Russia's Krasnodar region overnight, with drone debris falling on an industrial facility in the town of Afipsky and sparking a fire; the exiled outlet Astra identified the target from eyewitness footage of smoke. The refinery processes 9.1 million tons of crude a year — around 3% of Russia's national total — produces gasoline and Euro-5 diesel, and was placed under EU sanctions in April. And on Thursday night Ukraine launched its fourth drone attack in a week on the Black Sea port of Tuapse, starting a fire at the seaport terminal.
Each side says the other's strikes prove its own case. Kyiv argues the nightly barrages on power plants, railways and ports — 78 strikes on energy facilities since around November 2, per DTEK — show Russia is trying to freeze Ukraine into submission as winter approaches, and Zelenskyy is pressing for more sanctions and synchronized pressure on Moscow. Moscow, which has not commented on the overnight barrage in the reporting so far, has framed its campaign as retaliation for Ukrainian refinery strikes, and Putin has vowed retaliation "twice over" for them. Ukraine, for its part, says hitting refineries and depots is meant to choke the oil revenue funding the war.
For ordinary Ukrainians, this is now a nightly routine with a winter edge: rolling blackouts across seven regions, emergency grid shutdowns in the Kyiv area, trains disrupted in Kharkiv, and apartment blocks burning in Odesa. No power plant in the country has gone undamaged, Zelenskyy has said, and the grid is being hit faster than crews can repair it. For Russians, the Afipsky and Tuapse strikes are part of a campaign that has repeatedly reached refineries deep inside Russia, squeezing fuel supply and export earnings.
In short: Russia fired 227 drones overnight, knocking out power in seven Ukrainian regions including Kyiv, while Ukraine struck the Afipsky refinery, hit Tuapse port for the fourth time in a week, and destroyed ammunition and fuel depots in occupied territory. Both sides are now openly trading energy-infrastructure strikes, and the grid — not the front line — is where the war is being felt most by civilians.
Sources:
Source: aljazeeranews-3fuh52rgrl.edgeone.app.

item.title: Apple: the first touchscreen Macs go on sale today — five new products at once
item.description:
Apple's first touchscreen Mac finally hits stores today. The 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display go on sale Friday, November 6, alongside three other new products: the OLED iPad mini, the M6 iMac and an M6 version of the regular 14-inch MacBook Pro. Apple announced all five across three days last month, wrapping up with its "Pro and Tell" event in Los Angeles on October 28, and preorders that began that day are now arriving.
The touchscreen MacBook Pro is the one stealing the spotlight. After years of Apple executives dismissing the idea, the new MacBook Pro is the first Mac with a touch display, and the first with a tandem OLED panel — which Apple calls PROLED XDR. The 14.2-inch and 16.3-inch screens go up to 2,000 nits of peak brightness for both HDR and SDR content, with a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio. Touch is built into the panel rather than added as a separate layer, and Apple has kept it restrained: it works alongside the keyboard and trackpad rather than turning the Mac into an iPad. The laptops are also slimmer and lighter — the 14-inch drops from about 3.5 to 3.0 pounds, the 16-inch from 4.7 to 4.0 — bring Dynamic Island to the Mac, and mark the return of the glowing Apple logo. The 14-inch starts at $2,899 with M5 Pro ($4,499 with M5 Max); the 16-inch starts at $3,399. The first reviews, published Thursday, praise the display — Notebookcheck measured about 2,085 nits of peak HDR brightness on its 14-inch review unit — but the price is the argument.
The other three products fill out the range. The 14-inch MacBook Pro with the new M6 chip starts at $1,999 with 16GB of RAM and 1TB of storage, delivers up to 30% faster graphics than its predecessor, drives two external 4K displays at up to 165Hz, and adds Apple's in-house N1 wireless chip for Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 and Thread — but it has no touchscreen and no OLED panel. The OLED iPad mini gets its biggest redesign in years: a larger 8.5-inch OLED panel with an optional nano-texture finish, upgraded speakers and the A20 Pro chip in a 5.4mm-thin body with IP67 water and dust resistance, for $699 — $150 more than the previous model. The 24-inch M6 iMac skips M5 entirely, jumping from M4 to M6 with up to a 12-core CPU and GPU, Wi-Fi 7, optional 2.5 Gigabit Ethernet and support for two external 6K displays, starting at $1,499 with no price rise.
Reviewers are split in a useful way. The case for the touchscreen models is the display itself — tandem OLED, 2,000 nits, touch built in, a lighter machine — and the case against is the $400 premium over the equivalent non-touch M5 Pro model, which buys a better screen and touch but not a newer chip: the OLED models still run M5 Pro and M5 Max, while the cheaper M6 MacBook Pro has the newer processor. The consensus emerging from the first reviews is that the M6 14-inch at $1,999 is the safer buy for most people, and the PROLED models are for video, AI and 3D work where the display earns its keep. Apple is rolling the new machines out in 30 countries and regions, with deliveries and retail availability from today.
For buyers, the practical picture is simple: if you want touch on a Mac for the first time ever, it's $2,899 and up starting today; if you want the newest chip at the lowest price, it's the M6 14-inch at $1,999; and the iPad mini and iMac both got their biggest upgrades in years, with the mini up $150 and the iMac flat at $1,499.
In short: Apple's five-product launch day is today — the first touchscreen MacBook Pro from $2,899, the M6 MacBook Pro from $1,999, the OLED iPad mini at $699 and the M6 iMac at $1,499. The touchscreen models win on display and lose on value: the $400 premium buys OLED and touch, not a newer chip, so the M6 model is the pick for most buyers.
Sources:
Source: cultofmac.com.
item.content:encoded:
Apple's first touchscreen Mac finally hits stores today. The 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display go on sale Friday, November 6, alongside three other new products: the OLED iPad mini, the M6 iMac and an M6 version of the regular 14-inch MacBook Pro. Apple announced all five across three days last month, wrapping up with its "Pro and Tell" event in Los Angeles on October 28, and preorders that began that day are now arriving.

The touchscreen MacBook Pro is the one stealing the spotlight. After years of Apple executives dismissing the idea, the new MacBook Pro is the first Mac with a touch display, and the first with a tandem OLED panel — which Apple calls PROLED XDR. The 14.2-inch and 16.3-inch screens go up to 2,000 nits of peak brightness for both HDR and SDR content, with a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio. Touch is built into the panel rather than added as a separate layer, and Apple has kept it restrained: it works alongside the keyboard and trackpad rather than turning the Mac into an iPad. The laptops are also slimmer and lighter — the 14-inch drops from about 3.5 to 3.0 pounds, the 16-inch from 4.7 to 4.0 — bring Dynamic Island to the Mac, and mark the return of the glowing Apple logo. The 14-inch starts at $2,899 with M5 Pro ($4,499 with M5 Max); the 16-inch starts at $3,399. The first reviews, published Thursday, praise the display — Notebookcheck measured about 2,085 nits of peak HDR brightness on its 14-inch review unit — but the price is the argument.

The other three products fill out the range. The 14-inch MacBook Pro with the new M6 chip starts at $1,999 with 16GB of RAM and 1TB of storage, delivers up to 30% faster graphics than its predecessor, drives two external 4K displays at up to 165Hz, and adds Apple's in-house N1 wireless chip for Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 and Thread — but it has no touchscreen and no OLED panel. The OLED iPad mini gets its biggest redesign in years: a larger 8.5-inch OLED panel with an optional nano-texture finish, upgraded speakers and the A20 Pro chip in a 5.4mm-thin body with IP67 water and dust resistance, for $699 — $150 more than the previous model. The 24-inch M6 iMac skips M5 entirely, jumping from M4 to M6 with up to a 12-core CPU and GPU, Wi-Fi 7, optional 2.5 Gigabit Ethernet and support for two external 6K displays, starting at $1,499 with no price rise.

Reviewers are split in a useful way. The case for the touchscreen models is the display itself — tandem OLED, 2,000 nits, touch built in, a lighter machine — and the case against is the $400 premium over the equivalent non-touch M5 Pro model, which buys a better screen and touch but not a newer chip: the OLED models still run M5 Pro and M5 Max, while the cheaper M6 MacBook Pro has the newer processor. The consensus emerging from the first reviews is that the M6 14-inch at $1,999 is the safer buy for most people, and the PROLED models are for video, AI and 3D work where the display earns its keep. Apple is rolling the new machines out in 30 countries and regions, with deliveries and retail availability from today.

For buyers, the practical picture is simple: if you want touch on a Mac for the first time ever, it's $2,899 and up starting today; if you want the newest chip at the lowest price, it's the M6 14-inch at $1,999; and the iPad mini and iMac both got their biggest upgrades in years, with the mini up $150 and the iMac flat at $1,499.

In short: Apple's five-product launch day is today — the first touchscreen MacBook Pro from $2,899, the M6 MacBook Pro from $1,999, the OLED iPad mini at $699 and the M6 iMac at $1,499. The touchscreen models win on display and lose on value: the $400 premium buys OLED and touch, not a newer chip, so the M6 model is the pick for most buyers.

item.title: Houthi / Saudi: drone aimed at Mecca region intercepted Friday morning
item.description:
The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted and destroyed a Houthi drone heading for Saudi Arabia's Mecca region on Friday morning, coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki said in a social media post, and a missile aimed at western Saudi Arabia was brought down earlier.
The coalition also intercepted two ballistic missiles fired toward Najran on Friday, with debris falling and damage being assessed. On Thursday it destroyed a ballistic missile aimed at the eastern region and two aimed at Riyadh.
The Houthis denied targeting Mecca or the surrounding region, saying their operations target Saudi oil facilities and military bases only — the coalition has previously accused them of launching drones toward Mecca and Medina. The Houthis also claimed a drone attack on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam on Thursday evening, saying it achieved its objective; the coalition has not confirmed that claim.
Inside Yemen, fighting persists around Taiz, where the governor said the city is under heavy shelling with residential neighbourhoods hit, medical supplies, water and fuel cut off, and a notable escalation around Jabal Saber and Jabal Habashi.
Source: aljazeeranews-3fuh52rgrl.edgeone.app.

item.title: Israel: Herzog still hasn't picked — decision Sunday, Eisenkot expected to get the nod
item.description:
President Isaac Herzog still has not assigned the mandate to form Israel's next government, and will announce his choice on Sunday, November 8.
After consultations ended Thursday with 67 lawmakers recommending Yashar! leader Gadi Eisenkot and 46 backing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Herzog said the tally did not settle who could actually assemble a viable coalition, given mutual vetoes between and within blocs, and that he would hold further personal talks with party leaders first. Reuters reports Eisenkot is expected to receive the mandate, but it is unclear whether he can build a majority: his 67 recommendations include the Arab-led Ra'am (8) and Joint List (11), whose backing is not the same as joining a coalition, and he has ruled out governing with either Arab party.
Netanyahu's bloc holds 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset; the new Knesset is sworn in Tuesday, November 10.
Source: securitysignal.co.uk.

item.title: Poland: nearly half of Poles say Tusk should resign after the tribunal takeover
item.description:
The first poll since Prime Minister Donald Tusk's takeover of the Constitutional Tribunal finds 47.4% of Poles say he should no longer serve as prime minister, against 38.3% who want him to stay and 14.3% undecided, in a Wprost survey reported Friday.
The takeover — judges elected by the current parliamentary majority suspending the court's president and vice president, lowering the quorum and assuming control, with riot police seizing the building — has split the country: a separate United Surveys poll published Tuesday found the largest group, 38.6%, believes neither side is right, with Nawrocki backed by 28.7% and Tusk's government by 26.6%. Meanwhile the government is pressing ahead: the head of the Prime Minister's Chancellery, Jan Grabiec, confirmed the administration will soon table a broad slate of legislative measures to the court, seeking to fast-track matters officials say have been stalled for years.
President Karol Nawrocki has called the takeover a "crime against the Constitution"; the two leaders still have no meeting date, and European Parliament President Roberta Metsola is due in Warsaw in the coming days.
Source: zerohedge.com.

item.title: WordPress CVE-2026-119977 — federal deadline TODAY, November 6
item.description:
The race-condition flaw in WordPress Core (versions 4.7.0–7.1.3, CVSS 8.1) lets unauthenticated attackers run code during a core upgrade, and CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on November 3 with a November 6 deadline for federal agencies.
Wordfence published fresh attack data on November 5: its firewall has now blocked more than 240,000 exploit attempts, peaking on October 30 with over 74,000 attempts in a day. The fix is WordPress 7.1.4 (with backported fixes for older branches) — update now if you run a site.
Source: brandefense.io.

item.title: Binance Recovery Update #9: more withdrawals reopened, and the proof-of-reserves is now live
item.description:
Binance reopened withdrawals for another 58 token-network pairs from 04:00 UTC on Friday, November 6 — the fourth batch since the October 29 theft — bringing the published total to 259 pairs across 151 tokens.
Native Cardano, Litecoin, Polkadot, Stellar and NEAR withdrawals are still only available as BNB Smart Chain tokens, not on their native networks. And the 44-token zero-knowledge proof-of-reserves snapshot from November 4 is now live, PANews reported Friday morning — users can verify for themselves that balances are backed at least 1:1, so the 98%-replenished figure is no longer just Binance's word.
The remaining ~2% of the ~$6.3B stolen is still being bought back through market and OTC channels.
Source: bitcoininsider.org.

item.title: Courts: Brand fallout — producer steps back, publisher pulls his books
item.description:
Russell Brand spent his first night behind bars after Thursday's convictions (one rape, three sexual assaults; sentencing Monday, November 9).
The fallout started Friday: TV production company Various Artists asked its head of comedy, Jack Bayles — named in court as present and laughing during one of the 2009 assaults — to step back from his job while it reviews the events, and publisher Pan Macmillan is withdrawing Brand's books from sale. The Metropolitan Police investigation continues into two additional rape allegations, with files submitted to prosecutors.
No fresh developments on the FTC v. Amazon cases, the Netanyahu trial or the Murdaugh retrial (next hearing November 13).
Source: chortle.co.uk.

item.title: Turkey ratifies the Mecca defence pact — Saudi Arabia now has a treaty ally on paper, but no troops yet
item.description:
Turkey's parliament ratified the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement on Thursday evening, voting 279 to 119 to approve the trilateral pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan that treats an attack on any one of the three as an attack on all three. The vote, reported by Reuters and the Associated Press, settles the question left open in the evening brief, when only one low-quality outlet had claimed ratification and the major wires had not confirmed it. The agreement was signed in Mecca on August 7 by President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, and it now goes to the Official Gazette before the president formally approves it.
The pact itself is 16 articles. Article 1 commits the signatories to use "all necessary means" to eliminate threats to each other's territorial integrity, and Article 2 says that if one party suffers an armed attack or military aggression, the others will immediately assist "utilising the full range of mutual assistance measures available to them" — language that deliberately mirrors NATO's Article 5. The other articles commit the three to joint training and exercises, intelligence sharing through secure channels, defence-industry cooperation and joint production, and a committee of their defence ministers and chiefs of staff. The secretariat will sit in Saudi Arabia, with retired Pakistani General Nauman Mahmood named as its first secretary-general for a three-year term. Under Article 16 the agreement stays in force indefinitely, with no party allowed to withdraw for the first 10 years and three months' written notice required after that. It also leaves the door open for other countries to join with the existing members' approval — Syria's government has already expressed interest.
The two sides of the argument are about what ratification actually changes. Critics, including some in Turkey's own parliament — the opposition CHP backed it, but the İYİ Party, the DEM Party and the YENİ Party voted against — have raised the obvious tension: Turkey is a NATO member, and committing its military to a second collective-defence pact raises questions about where its forces and loyalties go if the two obligations ever clash. Turkish officials have dismissed that concern as unfounded, and the pact's own text is written to blunt it: the collective-defence clause is not automatic, decisions are taken by consensus after consultation, and each party acts within its own constitutional obligations. Defence Minister Yaşar Güler said in October that Turkish support would be about "strengthening deterrence," adding: "We absolutely do not foresee entering into any conflict with the Houthis." Under Article 92 of Turkey's constitution, sending troops abroad still needs a separate parliamentary vote, and the AK Party's Fuat Oktay stressed during the debate that ratification does not mean troops are sent automatically.
That matters because the other two members have already drawn their own lines. Pakistan has refused to join strikes inside Yemen, and Egypt — whose parliament approved sending military support in October — says any mission would be defensive only. The US has so far declined to offer direct support against the Houthis after its own weekslong campaign against the group in 2025. So Riyadh now has a ratified treaty with two partners, but neither partner has committed to fight on the ground in Yemen, and the Houthis are still about 50 miles from Aden, closer than at any time since 2015.
For ordinary people, the pact lands in the middle of a war that is already disrupting daily life in the kingdom. The Houthis attacked Saudi targets almost every day in October, hitting civilian airports and Aramco facilities, and the conflict monitor Acled recorded 26 incidents in the kingdom in recent days alone. Riyadh's King Khalid airport has been repeatedly hit and partly closed, airlines have cancelled flights for weeks, and on Thursday Saudi Arabia issued alerts warning of potential danger in Yanbu, the Red Sea oil export hub. Inside Yemen, fighting since July has killed and wounded thousands and displaced more than 250,000 people, according to the UN.
In short: Turkey has now ratified the Mecca pact, 279–119, giving Saudi Arabia a treaty that says an attack on one member is an attack on all — but the clause is not automatic, troops need a separate vote, and neither Turkey nor Pakistan has agreed to fight in Yemen. It is a deterrent on paper while the Houthis keep firing and Riyadh keeps waiting for an ally willing to act.
Sources:
Source: cdn.theturkiyetimes.com.

item.title: Ukraine: Russia's energy campaign is running at a pace unseen all war
item.description:
Ukraine's largest energy company DTEK says Russian forces struck Ukrainian power plants and electricity transmission facilities 78 times since around November 2 — compared with 11 such strikes in all of 2022 — according to the Institute for the Study of War's November 5 assessment.
Three DTEK power plants suspended operations after the November 3 strikes, and Kyiv's water outage that day was the most serious since the war began. The November 4–5 overnight barrage itself — 128 drones (65 of them jet-powered) and two Kh-35 missiles — killed a woman in the Sumy region and injured several people elsewhere, including one man at a logistics facility fire in Sofiivska Borshchahivka outside Kyiv; air defences downed or suppressed 105 of the drones.
No new overnight barrage has been reported yet for November 5–6.
Source: understandingwar.org.

item.title: Poland: von der Leyen publicly snubs Nawrocki at Visegrad summit
item.description:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen skipped a joint press conference with Polish President Karol Nawrocki at the Visegrad Group presidential summit in Trenčín, Slovakia, Bloomberg reported on Thursday — a public show of support for Prime Minister Donald Tusk in the Constitutional Tribunal crisis.
Von der Leyen reportedly considered boycotting the summit altogether before deciding that would attract more attention. Meanwhile Tusk's coalition partner PSL has proposed a constitutional reset to resolve the standoff, and European Parliament President Roberta Metsola is due in Warsaw in the coming days for separate meetings with both Nawrocki and Tusk.
The Tusk–Nawrocki one-to-one meeting still has no date.
Source: hungarianconservative.com.

item.title: Google CodeMender:
item.description:
Google unveiled an autonomous code-security agent at its Cloud Security Summit on Thursday — an agent that reviews code as autonomous coding agents commit it faster than humans can keep up.

item.title: Chrome 157 fixes 213 flaws, including 7 critical
item.description:
Google's Chrome 157 stable release (157.0.8103.38/.39) fixes 213 vulnerabilities, seven of them critical.
Separately, in-the-wild exploitation has been reported for CVE-2026-119264, a use-after-free in Dawn (Chrome's WebGPU implementation), CVSS 8.8, that could let a crafted page run code outside the sandbox — the report is logged by BSI CERT-Bund, the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security and Malwarebytes Labs, though Google itself reported no known in-the-wild exploitation for the 157 batch. Update Chrome (and Edge) and make sure the browser restarts.
Source: cvetodo.com.

item.title: Apache OFBiz critical code injection (CVE-2026-83542)
item.description:
A remote unauthenticated attacker can execute code on OFBiz 24.09 before 24.09.08 by staging crafted widget XML through a multipart upload.
No exploitation has been recorded, but two earlier OFBiz CVEs are already in CISA's KEV catalog — patch if you run it.
Source: cvetodo.com.

item.title: Binance Recovery Update #8:
item.description:
Binance restored withdrawals for 62 tokens (69 network-asset pairs) from 04:00 UTC on November 5, and says replenishment is still at about 98% of the ~$6.3B stolen.
The 44-token zero-knowledge proof-of-reserves snapshot from November 4 is still computing — due around November 6–7 — so the 98% figure remains Binance's own claim until the proof lands. Elliptic's November 5 count has $3.35B of the loot still sitting in attacker-linked addresses (up from $3.21B on November 4, because its address set changed) and $2.85B frozen or seized — single-vendor figures, treat them as one tracker, not a settled total.
Source: binance.com.

item.title: The tankers keep getting hit while Washington argues about whether to bomb Iran again
item.description:
Iran reported three more tankers damaged in the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday, and the attacks on Gulf shipping are now running at close to a record pace — at least five vessels have reported incidents since Sunday, according to the UK maritime security agency UKMTO, about the same rate as October, when 35 vessels were hit, the most of any month of the war. The UKMTO said one vessel was struck by two unidentified projectiles late on Wednesday. Iran's Revolutionary Guards, who don't usually admit to firing on merchant ships but say the transit route is unsafe without Tehran's consent, said two tankers had struck naval mines and another had caught fire on Thursday. The morning brief's tanker hit near Qatar — two projectiles about 50 nautical miles north of Madinat ash Shamal — was one of the week's incidents.
The politics around the war are now being fought in public. Vice President JD Vance said in a long social media post on Wednesday that the war was to blame for the Republicans' midterm defeat, and a White House adviser told Reuters that some officials inside the White House saw the post as a foreign policy break from the president and a public recognition of the war's economic cost. Iran's Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf mocked Vance on Thursday, accusing him of letting Trump double down like a "losing gambler" by planning more US strikes, and telling him: "Skip the TED talk. Why not say this to your boss?" Trump, asked about Vance's comments on Wednesday, defended launching the war as necessary to stop Iran getting a nuclear weapon — a justification he has used repeatedly.
But two sources told Reuters they believed Trump was still likely to order resumed hostilities. "He is planning to bomb Iran. Don't listen to what he's saying. He held off because of the midterms. We asked him to hold off until the midterms," one said; the other said Trump had nothing to lose politically now that the midterms were over. That sits against what Trump said Wednesday — no immediate new large-scale strikes, "locked and loaded if we need to go, but there may be no reason for it" — and against the military preparations Axios reported, with more assets being sent to the region and no final decision made. On Wednesday, Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei said there should not be "even the slightest inclination towards submission" to the United States, which he said would remain hostile no matter which party was in power. Qatar said Tuesday that both sides were committed to mediation and reviewing proposals, but a senior Iranian official said this week the two sides remain far apart, and neither side has announced any breakthrough on the big issues: the future of the strait, the US blockade on Iranian ports, sanctions, and a resumption of nuclear talks.
For ordinary people, the clearest signal is still the oil price. Prices have plunged in recent days as traders bet that Trump, chastened by voters, may be less likely to restart the strikes he launched alongside Israel as "Operation Epic Fury" in February. They bounced back slightly on Thursday but are still down more than $20 a barrel from last week. The morning brief's numbers still stand: Brent was at $95.07 on Thursday, down almost 10% in a week, while US diesel is running about $6.27 a gallon — roughly 75% higher than a year ago — with reserves below 100 million barrels for the first time in more than 20 years.
In short: the shooting in the Gulf hasn't stopped — three more tankers Thursday, a record pace — while Washington argues in public about whether the war cost Republicans the election, and Trump, who says there may be no reason to strike again, is still being described by sources close to him as likely to do exactly that. The Qatar mediation is the only off-ramp on the table, and nobody is claiming it's close.
Sources:
Source: reuters.com.

item.title: The Houthis' price to stop: $51 billion — and recognition as Yemen's rulers
item.description:
Saudi Arabia reached out to the Houthis to ask what it would take to stop the fighting, and the answer, according to the Wall Street Journal on Thursday, was $51 billion — the sum the Houthis say covers years of Saudi strikes and a long blockade — plus formal recognition as the rulers of Yemen. People briefed on the discussions said other figures have come up since, but the message was clear: the price of an exit would be in the tens of billions of dollars. The demand landed after the Houthis attacked Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea and seized territory commanding the Bab al-Mandeb chokepoint, and as they press toward Aden, the seat of Yemen's internationally recognized government, moving to within about 50 miles of the city — closer than at any time since 2015.
The two sides don't even agree on whether the demand was made. In a post on X on Thursday after the Journal's article appeared, Rayed Krimly, Saudi Arabia's deputy minister for public diplomacy, denied that the Houthis demanded money from Riyadh, calling them militias that "have revolted against the Yemeni government, caused the starvation of the Yemeni people and plunged Yemen into conflicts and agendas that do not serve Yemen and its people." The Houthi leadership didn't respond to requests for comment. The Journal, citing people briefed on the discussions, stands by the figure — and analysts quoted in the piece say the money may be the smaller problem: paying it would set a precedent where the group can escalate militarily whenever it wants more concessions, said Maged Al-Madhaji of the Sana'a Center for Strategic Studies.
Meanwhile the shooting hasn't paused. On Thursday, the Saudi-led coalition said it destroyed a ballistic missile fired toward the kingdom's eastern region, and later said two ballistic missiles launched toward Riyadh were also intercepted and destroyed, according to Al Jazeera. That followed Wednesday's Houthi claim of a ballistic missile at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport during Syria's President Ahmed al-Sharaa's visit — unconfirmed by Saudi authorities, with the airport kept operating — and Thursday morning's Saudi alerts warning of potential danger in Yanbu, the Red Sea oil export hub. Inside Yemen, the Journal reports a Houthi strike in Shabwah governorate killed at least 75 people and wounded more than 200, the deadliest since the civil war reignited, and the Houthis have been targeting areas that would serve as muster points for any Saudi-led ground attack.
Riyadh's options are all bad, and the Journal lays them out plainly. Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman doesn't want to negotiate fully with the Houthis without gains on the ground to use as leverage, Saudi officials said, but worries that sending more Saudi troops into Yemen could be bloody and spark anger at home — and there have already been dozens of casualties the authorities haven't reported publicly. The main outside ally the kingdom once had in Yemen, the UAE, withdrew entirely from the anti-Houthi campaign last December after a falling-out with Riyadh. Saudi Arabia has instead sought help through its new Mecca Pact with Turkey and Pakistan, which treats an attack on one as an attack on all — but Turkey's parliament has yet to approve it (it passed only the first article of the ratification bill on Wednesday before adjourning), Pakistan has refused to join strikes inside Yemen, and Egypt, whose parliament approved sending military support in October, says any mission would be defensive only. The US, meanwhile, has so far declined to offer direct support against the Houthis after its own weekslong campaign against the group in 2025.
For ordinary people, the war is measured in closed airports, cancelled flights and displacement. The Houthis carried out a near-daily campaign of attacks on Saudi Arabia in October, hitting civilian airports and Aramco facilities, and there have been 26 reported incidents in the kingdom in recent days alone, according to the conflict monitor Acled. Inside Yemen, fighting since July has killed and wounded thousands and displaced more than 250,000 people, according to the UN.
In short: Saudi Arabia asked the Houthis what it would cost to stop, and the answer — $51 billion and recognition as Yemen's government — is a price Riyadh hasn't agreed to and one Saudi official publicly denies was even demanded. With no ally willing to fight on the ground and the Houthis 50 miles from Aden, the kingdom is stuck between paying, fighting a war it can't win cheaply, or waiting.
Sources:
Source: wsj.com.

item.title: Israel: Eisenkot wins the recommendations, Herzog names his pick on Sunday
item.description:
President Isaac Herzog finished consultations with every Knesset faction on Thursday evening and said he intends to assign the mandate to form a government this coming Sunday, November 8. Factions representing 67 lawmakers recommended Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot; factions representing 46 recommended Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu; and United Torah Judaism, with seven seats, declined to recommend anyone. The Joint List, with 11 seats, announced Thursday it would recommend Eisenkot, joining Ra'am's eight — though both Arab-led lists' endorsements don't commit them to joining his coalition, and Eisenkot, like Netanyahu, has ruled out governing with them.
The arithmetic is the trap. Eisenkot's 67 recommendations are not 67 votes for a government: his core bloc of four Jewish-led parties won only 48 seats, the Arab-led lists won 19, and a majority needs 61 of 120. Netanyahu's bloc won 53 seats in the October 27 election, with Likud the largest single party at 27. Herzog said he still needs to clarify directly with some party leaders who can actually assemble a governing majority, which is why he is taking until Sunday rather than announcing immediately — he has until November 11. The new Knesset is sworn in on November 10, and whoever gets the mandate has 28 days to form a government, with a possible 14-day extension.
Netanyahu, at risk of losing power, has seized on an investigation by election officials into possible vote tampering to cast doubt on the results, accusing Arab-led parties of stealing the vote — a charge his critics say is an attempt to undermine results he denies trying to undermine. Israel's Central Election Committee said on Wednesday that the election's integrity had not been compromised, and its head, Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, called on elected officials to protect public trust rather than shake it. "This is a real danger. One of the foundations of democracy is the peaceful transfer of power," Sohlberg told Herzog. Netanyahu's far-right allies, including National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, have called for the immediate arrest and interrogation of Arab party leaders.
For ordinary Israelis, the stakes are a caretaker government running the country while the region stays volatile — Netanyahu remains prime minister until a new coalition is formed, or through another election if no candidate succeeds — and a president openly warning parties to do their utmost to avert another round of voting. Herzog told the factions that "any reasonable person need only look at the security and diplomatic challenges before us, at the changing region around us, and remember the issues tearing us apart from within, to understand that an immense responsibility rests upon us."
In short: Eisenkot has the recommendations, 67 to 46, and Herzog will name his pick on Sunday — but recommendations aren't a coalition, and with both men ruling out governing with the Arab parties whose backing put Eisenkot ahead, nobody has shown a path to 61 seats yet. Netanyahu is fighting the result itself, and another election is still on the table.
Sources:
Source: wncy.com.

item.title: Ukraine: aid-centre death toll reaches 42 as Brussels talks turn to security guarantees
item.description:
The death toll from Monday's Russian bombing of an aid distribution point in the village of Komyshuvakha, in the Zaporizhzhia region, has risen to 42, police said on Thursday, making it one of the deadliest strikes on civilians this year. Up to 33 people remained buried beneath the rubble, with rescue work continuing and bodies still being identified. On Wednesday, regional official Ivan Fedorov had said 59 people were missing. Bodycam footage from one of the police officers killed, which Reuters verified, showed the moments before a second Russian strike hit, destroying the shelter where residents were hiding after a radio warning. Ukraine's national police said the strikes included a 3-ton FAB glide bomb, carrying around 1.4 tons of explosives. Russia's Defence Ministry said the attack targeted Ukrainian military units around Komyshuvakha and two other settlements, and that up to 25 Ukrainian servicemen were killed. Both Moscow and Kyiv deny deliberately targeting civilians; the UN human rights mission in Ukraine said on Tuesday that the bombing likely violated international law.
At the same time, the diplomacy track moved to its second day in Brussels. Talks on Ukraine's postwar reconstruction and security guarantees resumed on Thursday at NATO headquarters, with delegations from Ukraine, the US, the UK, France, Germany, the EU and NATO, plus the World Bank and the US investment group BlackRock, according to the Associated Press. Ukraine's lead negotiator Rustem Umerov said the discussions covered postwar reconstruction, funding for 2027 and the security guarantees Western allies could offer, as well as a new post-war European security architecture. US envoy Jared Kushner called the talks "productive and substantive" in a post on X. The Brussels meetings come a week before negotiators from Russia, Ukraine and the US are due to meet in Abu Dhabi on November 10-11.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, speaking from an Ibero-American summit in Spain, said in an interview broadcast Thursday that Ukraine must adapt to the new realities of US politics after the Democrats won both chambers of Congress, and that solving the Patriot air-defence issue is the top priority — he is also working to keep enough F-16 fighter jets operating over the next five to six months. He said EU, NATO and US officials meeting in Brussels were making some progress on security-guarantee proposals. Overnight, Russia said it struck logistics and transport targets across Ukraine, including a Nova Poshta logistics hub in Kharkiv region that Moscow said was used to assemble drones, railway locomotives, a power station in Dnipropetrovsk region, and a cargo vessel at sea off Odesa — claims Reuters could not independently verify.

item.content:encoded:
The death toll from Monday's Russian bombing of an aid distribution point in the village of Komyshuvakha, in the Zaporizhzhia region, has risen to 42, police said on Thursday, making it one of the deadliest strikes on civilians this year. Up to 33 people remained buried beneath the rubble, with rescue work continuing and bodies still being identified. On Wednesday, regional official Ivan Fedorov had said 59 people were missing. Bodycam footage from one of the police officers killed, which Reuters verified, showed the moments before a second Russian strike hit, destroying the shelter where residents were hiding after a radio warning. Ukraine's national police said the strikes included a 3-ton FAB glide bomb, carrying around 1.4 tons of explosives. Russia's Defence Ministry said the attack targeted Ukrainian military units around Komyshuvakha and two other settlements, and that up to 25 Ukrainian servicemen were killed. Both Moscow and Kyiv deny deliberately targeting civilians; the UN human rights mission in Ukraine said on Tuesday that the bombing likely violated international law.

At the same time, the diplomacy track moved to its second day in Brussels. Talks on Ukraine's postwar reconstruction and security guarantees resumed on Thursday at NATO headquarters, with delegations from Ukraine, the US, the UK, France, Germany, the EU and NATO, plus the World Bank and the US investment group BlackRock, according to the Associated Press. Ukraine's lead negotiator Rustem Umerov said the discussions covered postwar reconstruction, funding for 2027 and the security guarantees Western allies could offer, as well as a new post-war European security architecture. US envoy Jared Kushner called the talks "productive and substantive" in a post on X. The Brussels meetings come a week before negotiators from Russia, Ukraine and the US are due to meet in Abu Dhabi on November 10-11.

item.title: N0n ransomware group published data from Delta Dental of Missouri and The Container Store on Thursday (unverified tracker claims)

The Container Store leak includes 46,013 customer chat messages, search-session analytics, 9,305 customer email addresses and a staff directory. Both are listed as "not paid — exposed."
The dental insurer leak is the serious one: SSNs plus health details is full identity-theft material.
Source: qpulse.quasarcybertech.com.

item.title: Open source: today's trending
item.description:
GitHub's trending list on Thursday is still dominated by agent tooling, with two notable new entries.
NVIDIA/auto-ontology (+2,707 stars) is a Python framework for building semantic, graph-based reasoning layers over data so AI agents query it with certified metric definitions instead of guessing. cloudflare/security-audit-skill is the strongest debut: installed as a skill, it has your coding agent map a codebase's architecture and trust boundaries, sends isolated hunter agents after the uncovered areas, and hands every candidate to a fresh verifier that tries to disprove it before anything reaches the report. Still climbing: storytold/craft-anything (+3,639/day, 14.5k stars), the reverse-engineering explainer; vercel-labs/agent-desktop (+2.5k/day), the computer-use CLI; and garrytan/gstack (139k stars), Garry Tan's exact Claude Code setup with 23 opinionated tools.
Source: trendar.org.

item.title: FTC v. Amazon (ads auction):
item.description:
The FTC and 22 state attorneys general filed an updated complaint on October 28, with the newly unredacted details announced November 5, alleging Amazon secretly raised the prices advertisers paid in its online search advertising auction — by up to 50% above auction results on ordinary days, and up to 250% on major shopping days like Prime Day and Black Friday.
One large food-and-beverage advertiser faced increases of more than 100% during Prime Day 2023, and Amazon internally acknowledged the increases were "destroying campaign performance." Amazon said it strongly disagrees with the claims and that the FTC "fundamentally misunderstands how advertisers operate."
The antitrust trial itself is set for March 29, 2027.
Source: searchenginejournal.com.

item.title: The secret strikes before the midterms — and the war that paused
item.description:
The United States was quietly bombing Iran in the weeks before Tuesday's midterm elections, and the White House worked to keep it that way. The Wall Street Journal reported Thursday that American forces carried out a series of limited, unannounced strikes against Iranian targets — missile launchers and other military equipment — in the run-up to November 3, with senior officials discussing the political cost of admitting the attacks were still going on. One operation took place on November 2, the day before Americans voted: US forces struck targets on Qeshm Island, near the Strait of Hormuz, after Iranian forces fired a surface-to-air missile at an American fighter jet, according to US officials. The Journal says the strikes were designed to limit Iran's military capability while avoiding casualties, and that Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio were part of the discussions, which President Trump approved.
The secrecy is the story. On November 2, the same day as the Qeshm strike, Trump told reporters American forces had "not been engaged in combat for months." The Journal reports administration officials worried that renewed attention to the Iran fighting would damage Republican prospects in the elections — and the elections went badly for them anyway. Democrats won control of both the House and Senate, and Vance has publicly denounced the war as the primary cause of the Republican defeats. Trump has since acknowledged the war contributed to the losses, particularly through gasoline prices, while defending his decision to launch it.
What happens next is genuinely undecided, and the two sides of the administration are pulling in opposite directions. Trump said Wednesday he has no immediate plans for new large-scale strikes, telling the Financial Times "we're locked and loaded if we need to go, but there may be no reason for it," and describing the situation as "a brilliant situation." But Axios reports the US military is finishing preparations for a possible resumption of major combat operations, sending more assets to the region, with no final decision made and even Trump's closest aides unsure what he will do. Qatari mediators, meanwhile, are working on a draft agreement that could head off a return to fighting and lead to direct talks in the coming days. Iran's position hasn't moved: its top security official, Mohsen Rezaei, called Washington's reply to Tehran's seven conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz "not convincing," and the strait stays shut until they are fully met.
For ordinary people, the clearest signal is at the pump. Brent crude fell to $95.07 on Thursday, down almost 10% in a week to its lowest in two months, as the threat of renewed strikes receded. But the damage from months of war is still in the system: EA WorldView reports US diesel reserves have fallen below 100 million barrels for the first time in more than 20 years, and diesel is running about $6.27 a gallon — roughly 75% higher than a year ago, close to an all-time record. Inside Iran, the crackdown continues: Tehran executed two more participants in January's nationwide protests on Wednesday, Amirhossein Maleki and Amirhossein Ebrahimi, sentenced to death over the killing of four police officers in Isfahan.
In short: Washington was fighting a war it wouldn't admit to before the election, the election punished it anyway, and now the choice is between a deal the Qataris are still trying to broker and a new round of strikes the military is already preparing for. Nothing is decided, and the fuel-price pain that helped cost Republicans the midterms hasn't gone away.
Sources:
Source: live.eastoranews.com.

item.title: Russell Brand found guilty of rape and three sexual assaults
item.description:
A jury at Southwark Crown Court in London found Russell Brand guilty on Thursday of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault, after nine hours and thirteen minutes of deliberations spread over three days. The 51-year-old comedian was acquitted of two other rape charges and one count of attempted indecent assault. Judge Joel Bennathan told Brand he faced a "significant custodial term," remanded him in custody, and set sentencing for Monday, November 9.
The convictions cover four of the six women who accused Brand of offences between 1999 and 2009. He was found guilty of raping a 21-year-old fan after meeting her at a 2009 stand-up show at the Hammersmith Apollo; of sexually assaulting a Capital Radio worker in a corridor in 2005; of sexually assaulting a Channel 4 worker during a forced massage in 2009; and of groping an MTV worker at a Soho bar party in 2004 — though the jury cleared him of orally raping that same woman in a toilet afterwards. He was acquitted of raping a woman after a 1999 Labour Party conference fringe show in Bournemouth, and of trying to drag an MTV worker into a toilet to indecently assault her in 2001.
The trial turned on consent, and the two sides told the jury opposite stories about the same facts. Brand testified that he had "misused" his fame "very, very selfishly" for sexual encounters in the past, but insisted he never engaged in non-consensual activity — "consent is fundamental, essential, necessary, and in many ways, more important than sex itself." His barrister, Ian Winter, argued the case was "thoroughly contaminated" by Channel 4's 2023 Dispatches documentary, saying the complainants only came forward at the programme's invitation and the publicity made a fair trial impossible. Prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones pushed back in closing, noting the six women did not know each other and had nothing to gain: no limelight, no documentary appearance, no compensation claims — only, she said, "perhaps some closure by coming before you and telling you their accounts of what happened to them so long ago."
For the women, the verdict ends a case that began with the 2023 joint investigation by The Times, The Sunday Times and Channel 4, and ran for three weeks of testimony in which Brand himself took the stand. Brand stood straight and still in the dock as the verdicts were read, closing his eyes when the rape conviction was announced, and told his wife Laura Gallacher "I love you" before being taken into custody. The Metropolitan Police told Sky News they are investigating Brand over other rape allegations made by two more women, so this may not be the last case.
In short: after a three-week trial and three days of deliberations, a jury believed four of the six women and disbelieved two of the most serious allegations — a mixed verdict that still leaves Brand, 51, facing a significant prison sentence on Monday.
Sources:
Source: usatoday.com.

item.title: Ukraine overnight: quieter night, but the refinery war goes on
item.description:
Russia launched 2 missiles and 128 drones at Ukraine overnight, with 105 shot down or neutralized, according to Ukraine's General Staff.
One person was injured in the Kyiv region when a Russian attack set a logistics facility ablaze. Ukraine hit back at the Ryazan oil refinery, where a drone attack set off a large fire — at least six hits recorded — injuring one person, damaging power lines and shattering windows at a school, prompting class cancellations.
Russia's Defence Ministry claimed 496 Ukrainian drones were intercepted. The toll from Monday's strike on the Komyshuvakha aid centre stands at 40 dead.
Today in Brussels, Ukraine, the US, France, Germany, the UK, NATO and the World Bank meet on a post-war prosperity plan, with a separate security-guarantees session on Thursday.
Source: byteseu.com.

item.title: Saudi Arabia warns Yanbu oil hub is in danger
item.description:
Saudi Arabia issued alerts on Thursday warning of potential danger in Yanbu, the kingdom's Red Sea oil export hub, as Houthi attacks continue.
The Saudi-led coalition said it destroyed a missile launched by the group towards Medina, and civil defence issued emergency alerts for Sharurah, near the Yemeni border. The Houthis had not claimed any attack on Thursday; on Wednesday they said they had attacked Riyadh's international airport while Syria's President Ahmed al-Sharaa was visiting — Saudi authorities have not confirmed it, and the airport kept operating.
Source: tbsnews.net.

item.title: Israel: Eisenkot now favourite for the mandate
item.description:
President Isaac Herzog's consultations moved decisively toward Gadi Eisenkot on Thursday.
United Torah Judaism — a Netanyahu ally in the previous five elections — declined to recommend any candidate, a major setback for the prime minister. The Arab-led Ra'am list endorsed Eisenkot, as did the Democrats, while Otzma Yehudit backed Netanyahu.
Herzog meets Likud and Eisenkot's Yashar party on Thursday evening to close the consultations, and has until November 11 to decide who gets the first 28 days to try to form a government. With 48 opposition seats plus 19 Arab-led recommendations, Eisenkot is now the favourite for the mandate — though a recommendation is not the same as a governing coalition, and he has ruled out governing with the Arab parties.
Source: reuters.com.

item.title: Cyber: the TV-box botnet built by the manufacturer
item.description:
Google and partners dismantled XCPE, a botnet hidden in the firmware of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes across 200+ countries — a catch-up from Google Threat Intelligence Group's November 2 report.
Google says with high confidence that the manufacturer, Videostrong Technology Co., intentionally built and ran the backdoor for financial gain, renting the boxes out for ad fraud, proxy traffic and malware delivery. The backdoor ran with system privileges, loaded only after first boot so it dodged certification checks, and reinstalled itself if removed.
Google took legal action against the command-and-control domains, banned Videostrong from making certified Android devices, and says the takedown also severed access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices.
Source: plume.com.

item.title: Cyber: WordPress upgrade flaw now has a public exploit
item.description:
A working public proof of concept for WordPress CVE-2026-119977 was published on GitHub on November 4.
The flaw is a race condition in WordPress Core's update process (versions 4.7 through 7.1.3) that lets an unauthenticated attacker run PHP code on the server. CISA added it to the exploited-vulnerabilities catalog on November 3, and Wordfence blocked more than 12,000 attacks in a 24-hour window.
The federal remediation deadline is tomorrow, November 6 — update to WordPress 7.1.4. No new CISA KEV additions on November 5; the catalog stands at 1,768 entries.
Source: threatdefence.com.

item.title: Russian strikes force Ukraine's nuclear plants to cut output as Kyiv's water comes back — and Zelensky briefs US envoys ahead of Abu Dhabi
item.description:
Ukraine's Energy Ministry said on November 4 that Russian strikes forced the country's nuclear plants to reduce output, Crisis.Zone reports, without naming the plants or saying how far output fell. The ministry said the return to nominal levels will be gradual, "as soon as energy workers restore the networks damaged by the shelling." The Kyiv Post's explanation, carried in the same report, is that strikes on substations and transmission lines — not on reactors — are what force the plants to throttle back, a pattern Kyiv is now framing as a European nuclear-safety issue.
The details behind that cut are stark. Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal said Russia used 289 drones, 17 ballistic missiles and 59 cruise missiles in the overnight attack of November 2–3, which grid operator Ukrenergo described as one of the most extensive on the energy system; energy facilities were hit more than 20 times in 24 hours. Three of DTEK's five thermal plants stopped generating, according to Reuters, and Shmyhal said Russia directed three drones at a substation critical to the Khmelnytskyi Nuclear Power Plant — a step he said Ukraine reported to the IAEA. Russia's Defence Ministry, by contrast, claimed it hit four power plants and two substations, according to the Institute for the Study of War — a claim that describes the same campaign from the attacker's side and does not address the civilian outages. By Wednesday morning, Ukrenergo had cancelled emergency outages in Kyiv and most regions, returning them to scheduled hourly cuts, but Kharkiv region stayed on emergency cuts and some regions faced rationing of up to 16 hours a day.
For ordinary people, the human impact is in the taps and the heating as much as the lights. Most of Kyiv went more than 24 hours without running water after the November 3 strikes cut power to water facilities — the Kyiv Independent called it the most serious water outage in Kyiv since the war began — before the city water utility said on November 4 that all pumping stations were operating normally again and network pressure had stabilised. Warming centres were set up in the hardest-hit Kyiv districts, a day after the city began connecting residential buildings to heating. On the other side of the front, Russian-installed authorities in occupied Crimea said Ukrainian strikes caused widespread emergency outages on November 4, affecting Sevastopol, Simferopol and Kerch, with a Sevastopol schedule of two hours of power followed by six without — though officials also cited an external technical incident, and the primary cause could not be independently verified.
Diplomatically, Wednesday filled in the run-up to Abu Dhabi. President Volodymyr Zelensky had a "very detailed" discussion with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, the Independent's live blog reports, covering air defence — including Patriot interceptors — and Ukraine's proposals, which he said have been given to the American side. The European Commission's Wednesday session in Brussels, EuropeSays reports, was about refining scenarios for Ukraine's post-war economic development and prosperity, following up on earlier Miami talks, with a separate security-guarantee session due Thursday. Zelensky said another Brussels meeting takes place Thursday. ISW's assessment, carried by Crisis.Zone, reads the Russian campaign as aimed at "inflicting increasing costs on Ukrainian society and coercing Ukraine into capitulating over the winter" — which is exactly what the nuclear-output cut, the water outage and the 16-hour rationing look like from the ground.
In short: no reactor was hit, but the grid around them was hit hard enough to throttle nuclear output, Kyiv's water is back after its worst outage of the war, Kharkiv is still on emergency cuts — and with Brussels meeting again Thursday and Abu Dhabi set for November 10–11, Zelensky's message to the US envoys was air defence first.
Sources:
Source: crisis.zone.

item.title: Riyadh airport kept operating on Wednesday despite the Houthi missile claim — while Tehran reads the US midterms as a vote against war
item.description:
Yemen's Houthis claimed on Wednesday that a ballistic missile "directly" hit King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, causing what spokesman Yahya Saree called significant damage, Demócrata reports, alongside the other Wednesday operations already covered in the evening brief. The counter-evidence arrived the same evening: flight tracking reviewed by The Contrail shows the airport operating on Wednesday, with no delays flagged and about 15 departures cancelled — in line with recent days — and Saudi Arabia has not confirmed any damage. Saree again urged airlines and passengers to avoid Saudi airspace except over Mecca and Medina.
The two sides' positions are now easy to state plainly. The Houthis say the airport is a military target and unsafe, and have claimed repeated hits on it since October 7–11, when attacks killed at least 20 people by one tally. The airlines' behaviour tells a different story from either claim alone: most foreign carriers are still staying away — Etihad has now extended its Riyadh cancellations through November 19, Air France to December 12, Cathay Pacific to January 31, and British Airways' return is reportedly set for January 11 — while Saudi airlines keep flying, Saudia having moved most of its Riyadh flights to other Saudi airports through about December 1. Australia escalated its travel advice in the same window, Smartraveller warning travellers not to visit Saudi Arabia's airports in the current volatility, the Houthis having named Aramco targets as well.
For ordinary people, the practical point is that "open" and "normal" are not the same thing in Riyadh right now: the airport is operating, but largely on Saudi airlines, with most foreign routes still suspended into November, December or beyond — and every new claim, confirmed or not, gives airlines another reason to push their return dates back. In Tehran, meanwhile, parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said Wednesday that the US midterm results reflected growing public opposition to the war against Iran, AnewZ reports — a political reading of an American election, not a change in the battlefield, where Iran's position remains that the Strait of Hormuz reopens only if Washington meets its seven conditions, a position Rezaei repeated as "not convincing" on Tuesday. No new US–Iran deal was announced Wednesday.
In short: the Houthis claimed a direct hit on Riyadh airport, the airport kept operating and Riyadh has not confirmed damage, foreign airlines keep pushing their returns back — and Tehran is spinning the midterms while holding its Hormuz conditions unchanged.
Sources:
Source: thecontrail.org.

item.title: Tencent Hy4 — a 770-billion-parameter model that can see and use a computer, but the weights aren't out yet:
item.description:
Tencent switched on the full Hy4 on November 4: a 770B-parameter mixture-of-experts model (49B active per token, 1M-token context) that, unlike the text-only August preview, can interpret images, charts and documents and operate software through graphical interfaces and command lines.
The catch the headlines skip: on launch day Hy4 is hosted only — through Tencent Cloud TokenHub, WorkBuddy/CodeBuddy, Yuanbao, ima and APIs on OpenRouter and others — with weights and a system card promised "in the coming days." Until they land, nobody outside Tencent can download, run or fine-tune it, so treat "open-source" here as announced, not yet delivered.
Tencent's own computer-use benchmark puts Hy4 at 78.9 on OSWorld 2.1, behind Claude Opus 5.5 at 81.8 in Tencent's table — company-reported, not independently reproduced. Sources:
Source: startupfortune.com.
